title: The Mask Is Not the Object: Volumetric Supervision for 3D Gaussian Segmentation
claim: A rendered mask can look correct while the underlying 3D selection is incomplete, which only a volumetric removal test reveals.
layout: Left scene photo; right two stacked pipeline panels, left-to-right, shaded second panel
description: The left side shows a row of multi-view photos of a stuffed-toy scene feeding into a 3D Gaussian scene. A dashed outline marks the queried 'Sheep' toy, and a search bar reads 'Sheep'. The right side has two stacked pipelines. (a) View-space evaluation: 3D Gaussian ellipsoids on axes, a prompt arrow, and a selection with some Gaussians greyed out. A camera then renders the sheep and a clean white-on-black mask. (b) Volumetric evaluation, on a cream-shaded background: the same Gaussians go through a prompt and a removal step. A camera renders depth, and the resulting heatmap is labeled 'incomplete' in red-orange, showing the sheep was only partly removed. The eye goes first to the large photo, then to the shaded panel (b) and its 'incomplete' label.
caption: A plausible rendered mask does not imply complete 3D selection. For the query "sheep," (a) the selected Gaussians render a plausible object mask, but (b) the depth change after removing the same Gaussian set indicates incomplete object removal in the reconstructed scene. This exposes a gap between rendered-mask quality and Gaussian-level selection completeness.
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting enables object-level operations on Gaussian primitives, yet existing segmentation methods are largely trained and evaluated through rendered views. This mismatch can produce accurate rendered masks from incomplete 3D selections since alpha-blended feature supervision concentrates learning on dominant contributors while leaving occluded or low-contribution Gaussians weakly supervised. We propose VODA, a plug-and-play supervision objective that exploits local depth structure to group per-pixel contributors and directly supervises all Gaussians in selected depth clusters, bypassing contribution-weighted gradient delivery. To evaluate volumetric completeness, we introduce Removal-3D, a synthetic object-removal benchmark, and the Removal Depth Error (RDE), a metric comparing predicted and ground-truth depth changes. Across four rendering-based baselines, VODA consistently improves volumetric segmentation on Removal-3D while maintaining or improving performance on LERF and ScanNet. Further analysis shows that VODA recovers lower-contribution Gaussians, while simple gradient reweighting and spatial propagation fail to reproduce comparable gains.
